# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach temperatures hot enough to vaporize rock on close-orbiting worlds, while the nightside plunges to frigid depths where atmospheres themselves may freeze out. On the exoplanet WASP-121b, dayside temperatures exceed 2,500°C, while some models suggest nightside temperatures hundreds of degrees cooler.

However, tidal locking doesn't necessarily doom a planet to climatic extremes. Atmospheric circulation can redistribute heat remarkably effectively. On temperate tidally locked worlds, winds transport energy from the dayside to the nightside, moderating temperatures on both sides. Climate models suggest that a sufficiently thick atmosphere—perhaps even a modest one like Earth's—could keep temperatures habitable across much of the planet's surface.

This heat transport creates distinctive climate patterns. Scientists predict a permanent "eye" of clouds at the substellar point, where intense heating drives convection and cloud formation.
